questions.question: Which of these is an XRPL address?
questions.why: Addresses start with r. The second is a ledger index, and the third is a 64-character transaction hash. All three are real, from lessons in this course.
wrongWhy: “107587014” does not follow from this evidence. Addresses start with r. The second is a ledger index, and the third is a 64-character transaction hash. All three are real, from lessons in this course.

“F3B8B18E6AEFDCEA3388D0B0932820C4F10F4849847E7989876FA9CD19687A70” does not follow from this evidence. Addresses start with r. The second is a ledger index, and the third is a 64-character transaction hash. All three are real, from lessons in this course.

questions.question: An account has 10 XRP and owns 5 objects. About how much can it spend?
questions.why: 1 XRP base reserve plus 5 × 0.2 XRP owner reserve locks 2 XRP, leaving 8.
wrongWhy: “10 XRP” does not follow from this evidence. 1 XRP base reserve plus 5 × 0.2 XRP owner reserve locks 2 XRP, leaving 8.
“5 XRP” does not follow from this evidence. 1 XRP base reserve plus 5 × 0.2 XRP owner reserve locks 2 XRP, leaving 8.

questions.question: A result starts with tec. What happened?
options: It failed but was recorded, and the fee was charged
questions.why: tec codes are recorded failures: nothing moved except the fee.
wrongWhy: “It succeeded” does not follow from this evidence. tec codes are recorded failures: nothing moved except the fee.
“It was never sent” does not follow from this evidence. tec codes are recorded failures: nothing moved except the fee.

questions.question: Where is a transaction's final result stored?
options: In its metadata, in a validated ledger
questions.why: Metadata records what actually happened once the ledger is validated.
wrongWhy: “In the sender's email” does not follow from this evidence. Metadata records what actually happened once the ledger is validated.
“In the Amount field” does not follow from this evidence. Metadata records what actually happened once the ledger is validated.

questions.question: What identifies a token on the XRPL?
options: Its currency code and its issuer address together
questions.why: Anyone can use the code USD. The issuer address is what makes it a specific token.
wrongWhy: “Its currency code alone” does not follow from this evidence. Anyone can use the code USD. The issuer address is what makes it a specific token.
“Its price” does not follow from this evidence. Anyone can use the code USD. The issuer address is what makes it a specific token.

questions.question: What must you open before you can hold a token?
options: A trust line to its issuer
questions.why: A TrustSet transaction opens the trust line that records your limit and balance.
wrongWhy: “A bank account” does not follow from this evidence. A TrustSet transaction opens the trust line that records your limit and balance.
“A payment channel” does not follow from this evidence. A TrustSet transaction opens the trust line that records your limit and balance.

questions.question: Weights: Alice 3, Bob 2, Carol 2. Quorum 5. What is the fewest people who can sign?
questions.why: Alice (3) plus Bob or Carol (2) reaches 5.
wrongWhy: “3” does not follow from this evidence. Alice (3) plus Bob or Carol (2) reaches 5.
“1” does not follow from this evidence. Alice (3) plus Bob or Carol (2) reaches 5.

questions.question: A treasury has a signer list, but its master key is still enabled. What is the risk?
options: One person with the master key can bypass the list
questions.why: An enabled master key can sign alone, skipping the signer list.
wrongWhy: “None, the list always wins” does not follow from this evidence. An enabled master key can sign alone, skipping the signer list.
“The account is blackholed” does not follow from this evidence. An enabled master key can sign alone, skipping the signer list.

questions.question: Where are an NFT's rules stored?
options: In a PDF from the seller
questions.why: The ID encodes the flags and the transfer fee the issuer set at minting.
wrongWhy: “In a PDF from the seller” does not follow from this evidence. The ID encodes the flags and the transfer fee the issuer set at minting.
“Nowhere, they are secret” does not follow from this evidence. The ID encodes the flags and the transfer fee the issuer set at minting.

questions.question: What does mutable mean for an NFT?
options: The issuer can change what it points to after you buy it
It can be split into pieces
questions.why: A mutable NFT's URI can change, so the picture or document can change.
wrongWhy: “It can be split into pieces” does not follow from this evidence. A mutable NFT's URI can change, so the picture or document can change.
“It is free” does not follow from this evidence. A mutable NFT's URI can change, so the picture or document can change.

questions.question: How does an amendment switch on?
options: 80% of validators support it for two weeks in a row
The first person to vote wins
questions.why: It needs a supermajority that holds for two weeks.
wrongWhy: “Ripple decides” does not follow from this evidence. It needs a supermajority that holds for two weeks.
“The first person to vote wins” does not follow from this evidence. It needs a supermajority that holds for two weeks.

questions.question: What is an XLS number?
options: The public proposal behind a feature
questions.why: For example, XLS-30 is the proposal for AMM pools.
wrongWhy: “A ledger index” does not follow from this evidence. For example, XLS-30 is the proposal for AMM pools.
“A type of fee” does not follow from this evidence. For example, XLS-30 is the proposal for AMM pools.

questions.question: What sets an AMM pool's price?
options: The ratio of the two balances in the pool
The last trade on another blockchain
questions.why: The pool prices trades from the ratio of what it holds.
wrongWhy: “Ripple” does not follow from this evidence. The pool prices trades from the ratio of what it holds.
“The last trade on another blockchain” does not follow from this evidence. The pool prices trades from the ratio of what it holds.

questions.question: Who votes on a pool's trading fee?
options: LP token holders, weighted by their LP tokens
questions.why: Voting power follows LP token holdings.
wrongWhy: “Validators” does not follow from this evidence. Voting power follows LP token holdings.
“The first depositor only” does not follow from this evidence. Voting power follows LP token holdings.

questions.question: What does KYC mean?
options: Know Your Customer: checking who a customer is
questions.why: KYC is identity verification.
wrongWhy: “Keep Your Coins” does not follow from this evidence. KYC is identity verification.
“A type of token” does not follow from this evidence. KYC is identity verification.

questions.question: What can behaviour screening NOT see?
options: What a token's issuer can still do
questions.why: Issuer powers are a property of the asset, stored in the issuer's flags.
wrongWhy: “Who sent a payment” does not follow from this evidence. Issuer powers are a property of the asset, stored in the issuer's flags.
“Sanctions lists” does not follow from this evidence. Issuer powers are a property of the asset, stored in the issuer's flags.

questions.question: What are NOSHASHI's two questions?
options: Am I allowed to move this? Could I actually get out of it?
What is the price? Should I buy?
Who is the CEO? Where is the office?
questions.why: Law and policy on one side, market reality on the other.
wrongWhy: “What is the price? Should I buy?” does not follow from this evidence. Law and policy on one side, market reality on the other.
“Who is the CEO? Where is the office?” does not follow from this evidence. Law and policy on one side, market reality on the other.

questions.question: What does NOSHASHI do when the ledger does not give enough to decide?
options: Says so, instead of guessing or showing zero
questions.why: It withholds the figure and explains why.
wrongWhy: “Shows zero” does not follow from this evidence. It withholds the figure and explains why.
“Guesses” does not follow from this evidence. It withholds the figure and explains why.

questions.question: Which screen should you glance at first to confirm you are connected?
questions.why: A climbing ledger number means a live, current connection.
wrongWhy: “Pricing” does not follow from this evidence. A climbing ledger number means a live, current connection.
“Settings” does not follow from this evidence. A climbing ledger number means a live, current connection.

questions.question: Which screen tells you how old a counterparty is and who funded it?
questions.why: Provenance traces an account's real age and first funder.
wrongWhy: “Order Book” does not follow from this evidence. Provenance traces an account's real age and first funder.
“Token Rights” does not follow from this evidence. Provenance traces an account's real age and first funder.

questions.question: What is four-eyes approval?
options: A second person must approve a policy change
questions.why: One person drafts, another approves; both are logged.
wrongWhy: “Two screens at once” does not follow from this evidence. One person drafts, another approves; both are logged.
“A type of freeze” does not follow from this evidence. One person drafts, another approves; both are logged.

questions.question: Why is an investigation's log hash-chained?
options: So entries cannot be quietly edited or removed
questions.why: Each entry includes the fingerprint of the one before.
wrongWhy: “To make it faster” does not follow from this evidence. Each entry includes the fingerprint of the one before.
“To hide it from auditors” does not follow from this evidence. Each entry includes the fingerprint of the one before.

questions.question: How are most XRPL accounts emptied?
questions.why: Fake sites, cloud notes, screenshots and malware expose secrets.
wrongWhy: “The ledger was hacked” does not follow from this evidence. Fake sites, cloud notes, screenshots and malware expose secrets.
“A validator stole it” does not follow from this evidence. Fake sites, cloud notes, screenshots and malware expose secrets.

questions.question: What is address poisoning?
options: Sending you a tiny payment from a look-alike address so you copy it later
questions.why: The fake sits next to the real address in your history.
wrongWhy: “A virus in the ledger” does not follow from this evidence. The fake sits next to the real address in your history.
“A freeze by the issuer” does not follow from this evidence. The fake sits next to the real address in your history.

questions.question: Someone offers to reverse your stolen XRP for a fee. What is it?
questions.why: Validated payments cannot be reversed by anyone.
wrongWhy: “A real service” does not follow from this evidence. Validated payments cannot be reversed by anyone.
“Ripple support” does not follow from this evidence. Validated payments cannot be reversed by anyone.

questions.question: What should you do first?
options: Move what is left to a new account made on a clean device
Post your seed online for help
questions.why: Whoever has the old key can take the rest at any moment.
wrongWhy: “Wait a week” does not follow from this evidence. Whoever has the old key can take the rest at any moment.
“Post your seed online for help” does not follow from this evidence. Whoever has the old key can take the rest at any moment.

questions.question: An escrow has matured. Does the XRP move by itself?
questions.why: Escrows wait for a finishing transaction.
wrongWhy: “Yes, automatically” does not follow from this evidence. Escrows wait for a finishing transaction.

questions.question: Which signature can hand control of your account to someone else?
options: Payment of 1 XRP to a friend
questions.why: SetRegularKey and SignerListSet give signing power away.
wrongWhy: “Payment of 1 XRP to a friend” does not follow from this evidence. SetRegularKey and SignerListSet give signing power away.
“TrustSet” does not follow from this evidence. SetRegularKey and SignerListSet give signing power away.

questions.question: Why are reserves alone not enough?
options: The business might owe customers more than it holds
questions.why: You need liabilities too, to work out coverage.
wrongWhy: “Reserves are always fake” does not follow from this evidence. You need liabilities too, to work out coverage.
“The ledger hides them” does not follow from this evidence. You need liabilities too, to work out coverage.

questions.question: A protection fund sits behind one key. How much does it count for?
options: Nothing, whoever holds the key can take it
questions.why: Only escrow or a real signer list makes a fund hard to take.
wrongWhy: “Everything” does not follow from this evidence. Only escrow or a real signer list makes a fund hard to take.
“Half” does not follow from this evidence. Only escrow or a real signer list makes a fund hard to take.

questions.question: Does ledger 108316232 tell you its close time?
options: Yes, convert the index into seconds.
No. Read the close-time field separately.
Only when the ledger has a payment.
questions.why: The index is a sequence number. Close time is a separate reported ledger field.
wrongWhy: The index counts ledgers, not seconds.
Payment contents do not turn a sequence number into a timestamp.

questions.question: Which evidence would you inspect before treating a payment as finalized?
options: The node’s validated status, transaction result and ledger reference.
questions.why: Current accepts changes; closed is awaiting validation; validated is the node-reported finalized ledger. A node reply is still a trusted source, not independent consensus verification.
wrongWhy: A sequence number alone does not establish validation.
Submitted does not mean validated.

questions.question: What should you do first with this payment evidence?
options: Inspect destination/tag and validation, then reconcile the delivered amount.
A successful engine result proves the invoice was fully paid.
questions.why: Reconcile only what metadata reports as delivered, after validation and destination/tag checks. A successful transaction can deliver less than requested.
wrongWhy: Requested amount is not evidence of actual delivery.
tesSUCCESS does not establish invoice amount, destination or tag agreement.

questions.question: What should you do first with this payment evidence?
options: Inspect destination/tag and validation, then reconcile the delivered amount.
A successful engine result proves the invoice was fully paid.
questions.why: Reconcile only what metadata reports as delivered, after validation and destination/tag checks. A successful transaction can deliver less than requested.
wrongWhy: Requested amount is not evidence of actual delivery.
tesSUCCESS does not establish invoice amount, destination or tag agreement.

questions.question: What should you do first with this payment evidence?
options: Inspect destination/tag and validation, then reconcile the delivered amount.
A successful engine result proves the invoice was fully paid.
questions.why: Reconcile only what metadata reports as delivered, after validation and destination/tag checks. A successful transaction can deliver less than requested.
wrongWhy: Requested amount is not evidence of actual delivery.
tesSUCCESS does not establish invoice amount, destination or tag agreement.

questions.question: The invoice expects 100 USD at destination A, tag 44. What can you conclude?
options: Hold reconciliation until destination and tag evidence is available.
Credit 100 USD to destination A now.
questions.why: Incomplete destination/tag evidence prevents invoice matching even when delivery and validation are known.
wrongWhy: Engine success is not invoice matching.
You cannot infer destination or tag from the amount.

questions.question: How much may you credit under this explicit training policy?
options: Nothing, because partial delivery always means failure.
questions.why: The training policy permits partial credit of the actual delivery after all matching checks. Keep the remaining shortfall visible.
wrongWhy: Requested 500 is not actual delivery.
This policy explicitly allows partial credit; protocols and business policies are different.

questions.question: What does NoFreeze not set establish?
options: The issuer may retain freeze authority under protocol rules.
questions.why: A control flag establishes a permission, not an event, solvency or wrongdoing.
wrongWhy: Permission is not evidence an action occurred.
Flags do not establish off-ledger reserves.

questions.question: Which question needs off-ledger evidence?
options: Does the issuer have legal redemption obligations?
questions.why: On-ledger flags can show authorization, freeze and clawback controls. Legal rights and reserves require separate evidence.
wrongWhy: Read the flag to establish whether it is set.
Read the flag; it does not describe a legal contract.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes these controls?
options: Freeze, clawback and authorization are the same setting.
Freeze can restrict token movement; clawback may reclaim eligible issued balances; authorization controls eligible holders.
questions.why: Each control has separate protocol constraints. None establishes reserves or legal rights.
wrongWhy: The flags and their effects differ.
Issued-token clawback is not native-XRP recovery.

questions.question: What is supported by this sell-side snapshot?
options: Funded depth is below the trade size; investigate before relying on an exit.
Funded depth covers this size in this snapshot; check fees, price impact and freshness before execution.
questions.why: Compare funded quantity, direction and the stated band to the trade size. A snapshot is not an execution guarantee.
wrongWhy: Funded quantity is below the stated size.
Quotes may be unfunded and conditions may change.

questions.question: What is supported by this sell-side snapshot?
options: Funded depth is below the trade size; investigate before relying on an exit.
Funded depth covers this size in this snapshot; check fees, price impact and freshness before execution.
questions.why: Compare funded quantity, direction and the stated band to the trade size. A snapshot is not an execution guarantee.
wrongWhy: Funded quantity exceeds the stated size in this example.
Quotes may be unfunded and conditions may change.

questions.question: What is supported by this sell-side snapshot?
options: Funded depth is below the trade size; investigate before relying on an exit.
Funded depth covers this size in this snapshot; check fees, price impact and freshness before execution.
questions.why: Compare funded quantity, direction and the stated band to the trade size. A snapshot is not an execution guarantee.
wrongWhy: Funded quantity is below the stated size.
Quotes may be unfunded and conditions may change.

questions.question: What should a reviewer receive for this training verdict?
options: HOLD, the failed rule, its evidence and the missing information.
A claim that HOLD means illegal.
A guarantee that a passed hash proves compliance.
questions.why: A policy result is a rule outcome within its evidence scope. Explain the rule, source, unknowns and proposed next step.
wrongWhy: A training policy is not a legal finding.
A hash is not a legal or compliance certification.

questions.question: What does this SHA-256 receipt establish?
options: Whether its contents match that digest, if recomputed.
questions.why: A digest checks consistency with contents. A party able to replace both contents and digest can replace both. It is not a digital signature.
wrongWhy: A digest does not authenticate an author.
Neither policy verdict nor hash proves reserves.
